subject: chemistry

moments.title: Crookes predicts a nitrogen crisis
moments.who: William Crookes, presidential address to the British Association
moments.body:
Sir William Crookes gives a famous address: 'The Wheat Problem'. He argues that the world's reliance on natural nitrogen fertilisers (Chilean nitrate, guano) cannot keep up with population growth. By the 1930s, he predicts, the world will face widespread famine unless chemists can fix atmospheric nitrogen.

The challenge is taken up across Europe. Several routes are tried: electric arc fixing (Birkeland-Eyde, Norway), calcium cyanamide (Frank-Caro, Germany), but all are too energy-intensive.
moments.takeaway: Civilisation's food supply is identified as a chemistry problem. The race is on.

moments.title: Haber demonstrates lab-scale ammonia synthesis
moments.body:
Haber demonstrates a tabletop apparatus that combines N2 and H2 over an osmium catalyst at high pressure (175 atm) and 550°C, producing droplets of liquid ammonia. The reaction is exothermic and gas-mole-reducing — Le Chatelier favours high pressure and low temperature, but only high temperature gives practical rates.

BASF buys the patent. Carl Bosch is assigned to scale it up.
moments.takeaway: A tabletop demonstration of the reaction every chemist had been chasing for two decades.

moments.title: Bosch builds the Oppau plant
moments.body:
Bosch and Alwin Mittasch screen thousands of catalyst formulations and settle on a promoted iron catalyst (with potassium and aluminium oxide promoters) — vastly cheaper than osmium. They engineer the high-pressure reactors, the gas-recirculation loops and the safety systems.

The Oppau plant begins producing ammonia at industrial scale in September 1913. By 1914 it produces 30 tonnes a day.
moments.takeaway: The largest chemical engineering project of its day — and a template for high-pressure synthesis ever since.

moments.title: Ammonia feeds the German war effort
moments.body:
When WWI begins, Britain's blockade cuts off German imports of Chilean nitrate. Ammonia from Haber-Bosch becomes the basis of explosives manufacture (via nitric acid and ammonium nitrate). Germany can fight on for four years rather than collapsing in months.

Haber also personally leads Germany's chemical weapons programme — chlorine gas at Ypres in April 1915, then mustard gas. His first wife Clara Immerwahr (also a chemist) shoots herself in May 1915 in apparent protest.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemistry sustains an industrial war. The same plant that makes fertiliser makes explosives.

moments.title: Two Nobel Prizes — Haber and Bosch
moments.body:
Haber wins the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The award is intensely controversial given his role in chemical warfare. Several past laureates boycott the ceremony.

Bosch wins the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Friedrich Bergius) for the engineering of high-pressure chemistry. Haber, of Jewish descent, is forced out of his Berlin institute by the Nazis in 1933 and dies in 1934 en route to Cambridge.
moments.takeaway: Recognition without resolution. The science and the moral weight remain entangled.

now.title: Ammonia today
now.body:
About 180 million tonnes of ammonia are made annually worldwide. About 80 percent goes to fertilisers — feeding an estimated 3.5 to 4 billion people. The process consumes about 1-2 percent of the world's total energy and emits roughly 1.4 percent of global CO2.

Hydrogen for the process comes overwhelmingly from steam reforming of natural gas (releasing CO2). 'Green ammonia' — using hydrogen made by electrolysis with renewable electricity — is a major research and engineering target. ITER-scale ammonia plants are being planned in Australia, Saudi Arabia and Chile.
now.open_questions: Can green ammonia scale and compete with fossil-fuel ammonia on cost? Can low-temperature catalysts replace the energy-hungry Haber-Bosch conditions? Can biological nitrogen fixation (the way legumes do it via nitrogenase) be engineered into cereal crops?

reflection: The Haber-Bosch process feeds half the world and was central to a war that killed 17 million people. Haber's first wife killed herself in apparent protest at his role in chemical weapons. How do we hold the simultaneous truth that a single scientist enabled both humanitarian benefit on a vast scale and unprecedented military destruction?
